title: The history of the tabla
tagline: About 2,000 years from drums made with river clay in an ancient Sanskrit text to a pair of small drums heard on Grammy stages, film soundtracks and drum machines.
intro: The tabla is a pair of drums: a small wooden one for the right hand and a big metal one for the left. Its secret is the black spot on each drumhead, a paste that turns a thud into a note. Drummers in India were loading drum skins with paste for centuries, the tabla itself took shape in the courts of 18th-century North India, and in 1920 a young physicist named C. V. Raman finally explained why it sings.

eras.name: Older drums and old ideas
eras.summary: Long before the tabla, Indian drummers played two-headed drums like the pakhawaj and mridangam. An ancient text already tells drum makers which earth and pastes to use on the skin.

eras.name: Born in the courts of Delhi
eras.summary: A new, lighter style of singing called khayal needs a new drum. In 18th-century Delhi, drummers split the job between two small drums and play with their fingertips.

eras.name: The six gharanas
eras.summary: Families of drummers move from Delhi to other cities and invent their own styles. Six schools, called gharanas, still shape how every tabla player learns.

eras.name: The science of the black spot
eras.summary: C. V. Raman shows that the loaded drumhead gives musical, harmonic overtones like a string. Later physicists work out the maths and watch drum makers tune a head layer by layer.

eras.name: Masters on stage and screen
eras.summary: Tabla players step out from the back of the stage to play solos, win national awards and shape the sound of Hindi film songs.

eras.name: Tabla goes global
eras.summary: The tabla reaches rock festivals, the Beatles, jazz fusion and electronic music. A Bangalore engineer builds a tabla machine, and Zakir Hussain becomes a world star.

events.title: A drummer carved in a cave
events.text: The Bhaja Caves are rock-cut Buddhist caves from about the 2nd century BCE. One carving shows a woman playing a pair of drums while another person dances. Some researchers, including the tabla player Aban Mistry, have pointed to it as a very early tabla-like pair, though it is not a tabla as we know it.
events.why: It shows that playing two drums side by side is a very old idea in India.

events.title: Rain on lotus leaves
events.who: The sage Svati, in a story told in the Natya Shastra (attributed to Bharata)
events.text: The Natya Shastra is an ancient Sanskrit guide to drama, dance and music. It tells how the sage Svati heard heavy rain drumming on lotus leaves and noticed high, middle and low sounds. The story says this gave him the idea for the first drums, which the text calls pushkaras.
events.why: It is one of the oldest stories anywhere about where the sound of a drum comes from.

events.title: An ancient recipe for drums
events.text: The Natya Shastra describes the pushkara drums in detail: their sizes, the woods and hides to use, and a blackish earth from riverbanks for the drum. It also mentions pastes put on the drum skins to sweeten the sound. Scholars date the text to somewhere between about 200 BCE and 200 CE.
events.why: It is the earliest written hint of the idea behind the tabla's black spot: putting something heavy on a drum skin to make it musical.

events.title: A famous legend with no evidence
events.text: A popular story says the poet Amir Khusrau invented the tabla around 1300 by cutting a drum in half. No painting, sculpture or document from his time supports it. Historians think the story may mix him up with a later musician with a similar name.
events.why: It is a good reminder that a story being famous does not make it true.

events.title: The pakhawaj, the tabla's big ancestor
events.who: Drummers of North Indian courts and temples
events.text: The pakhawaj is a long barrel drum with a skin at each end, played lying on its side. It became the drum of dhrupad, a grand and serious style of singing. Its bass head gets a dab of wheat dough before playing, and its treble head carries a black paste spot, like the south Indian mridangam.
events.why: Many tabla strokes and compositions were first played on the pakhawaj.

events.title: A music-loving emperor
events.text: Muhammad Shah ruled from Delhi from 1719 to 1748 and was nicknamed Rangila, the colourful one, for his love of the arts. At his court the khayal style of singing flourished under musicians like Niamat Khan Sadarang. Khayal is lighter and more flowing than dhrupad, and it suited a lighter drum.
events.why: The music of his court helped create the demand that the tabla would fill.

events.title: The first tabla school
events.text: Sidhar Khan Dhadi is the earliest name linked to the tabla in historical records. He is said to have been a pakhawaj player who developed a gentler way of playing with just two fingers near the edge of the drum. His followers became the Delhi gharana, the oldest of the tabla schools.
events.why: His crisp, fingertip style is what makes the tabla sound different from the booming pakhawaj.

events.title: The tabla appears in paintings
events.text: Clear pictures of the tabla only appear from about 1745 onwards. Historians such as James Kippen use evidence like this, not legends, to date the drum. Its shape kept changing until the early 1800s.
events.why: Pictures give the best evidence we have that the tabla took shape in the 18th century.

events.title: Two brothers move to Lucknow
events.text: Drummers from Sidhar Khan's family moved from Delhi to Lucknow, invited by the Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula. There they played for Kathak dancers and for singers at court. Their style grew bolder and more resonant to match the dance.
events.why: The Lucknow gharana showed the tabla could power dance as well as song.

events.title: Seven nights for the Nawab
events.text: Ram Sahai went from Benares to Lucknow as a boy to learn from Modhu Khan. At about 17 he is said to have played for the new Nawab for seven nights in a row. Back home in Benares he spent months working out a new, powerful style, which became the Benares gharana.
events.why: The Benares style could accompany soft singing and thunderous dance alike, and it is still one of the most played.

events.title: A village near Meerut gets its own style
events.text: Kallu Khan and Miru Khan learned from Sitab Khan, a master of the Delhi gharana, and took his teaching home to their village of Ajrara. There they built longer, trickier patterns of spoken drum syllables, called bols. Their school is called the Ajrara gharana.
events.why: It showed how one tradition can branch into new styles.

events.title: The Farukhabad gharana
events.text: Haji Vilayat Ali Khan learned from several masters and blended their ideas into a new style named after his home town. His title Haji is said to come from making the pilgrimage to Mecca several times. He is remembered for winning a tabla contest said to have lasted 15 days.
events.why: It became the youngest of the six classic schools and mixed ideas from the older ones.

events.title: Pakhawaj music moves to the tabla
events.who: Lala Bhavani Das, then Qadir Bakhsh and Fakir Bakhsh
events.text: In Punjab a famous pakhawaj tradition began with Lala Bhavani Das. Later players in Lahore, including Qadir Bakhsh and Fakir Bakhsh, moved its big, bold compositions onto the tabla. This became the Punjab gharana, the school of Alla Rakha and Zakir Hussain.
events.why: It carried the power of the old pakhawaj into the new drum.

events.title: Raman hears harmonics in a drum
events.who: C. V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar
events.text: Most drums ring with messy, unmusical overtones. Raman and Kumar wrote in the journal Nature that Indian drums like the tabla and mridangam are a remarkable exception. The loaded drumhead gives overtones in a neat harmonic series, just like a violin string.
events.why: It was the first scientific explanation of why the black spot turns a drum into a tuned instrument, and Raman went on to win the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for separate work on light.

events.title: Five tones from one drumhead
events.text: In the first volume of the Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences, Raman described the drums in more detail. He showed that the drumhead can split into patterns that act like a string divided into one, two, three, four or five parts. That gives five tones in harmonic order, while the higher, messier tones die away.
events.why: It turned drum makers' old craft into physics anyone could test.

events.title: The wizard of 'na dhin dhin na'
events.text: Anokhelal Mishra of the Benares gharana was nicknamed Jadugar, the wizard. He could play the pattern 'na dhin dhin na' clearly at astonishing speed. He played on All India Radio and with great musicians like Ali Akbar Khan and Vilayat Khan, but died young at 44.
events.why: His clarity at speed set a standard that tabla students still chase.

events.title: The tabla as a solo star
events.text: For centuries the tabla mostly accompanied singers and dancers. Ahmed Jan Thirakwa of the Farukhabad gharana became famous for playing it as a solo instrument. In 1954 he received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, India's top national honour for performers, and in 1970 the Padma Bhushan.
events.why: He showed audiences that a tabla player could hold a stage alone.

events.title: The maths of a loaded drumhead
events.who: B. S. Ramakrishna and M. M. Sondhi
events.text: Ramakrishna and Sondhi treated the tabla head as a composite membrane: a light skin with a heavier disc in the middle. Their calculations showed that the right size and weight of disc makes the first several modes almost harmonic. They published it in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America.
events.why: It explained with maths what Raman had heard, and later researchers still start from it.

events.title: Benares tabla abroad
events.text: Kishan Maharaj of Benares was famous for dazzling cross-rhythms and endings called tihais. In 1965 he played at the Edinburgh Festival and the Commonwealth Arts Festival in Britain. India later gave him the Padma Vibhushan, one of its highest civilian honours, in 2002.
events.why: He helped take the grand Benares style to audiences outside India.

events.title: Tabla on a Beatles album
events.who: George Harrison with musicians of the Asian Music Circle, including Natwar Soni
events.text: George Harrison recorded 'Within You Without You' for the Beatles album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. Indian musicians from London's Asian Music Circle played dilruba, swarmandal and tabla. The tabla player, Natwar Soni, was only publicly identified decades later.
events.why: Millions of rock fans heard the tabla on one of the best-known albums ever made.

events.title: A tabla solo at a rock festival
events.who: Ustad Alla Rakha with Ravi Shankar
events.text: At the Monterey International Pop Festival, Ravi Shankar played sitar with Alla Rakha on tabla. Alla Rakha's fast, fiery solo thrilled a crowd of rock fans, and the live album became Shankar's best-selling record. Two years later, on 15 August 1969, they played Woodstock in the pouring rain.
events.why: It made the tabla famous with a whole new generation in the West.

events.title: The beat of Hindi film songs
events.text: Samta Prasad of the Benares gharana played tabla for Hindi films such as Meri Surat Teri Aankhen (1963) and Sholay (1975). The composer S. D. Burman is said to have held up a recording until he could travel from Benares. Film composers R. D. Burman and Bappi Lahiri were among his students.
events.why: Through film songs, the tabla became a sound nearly everyone in India knows.

events.title: Shakti: tabla meets jazz guitar
events.who: John McLaughlin, L. Shankar, Zakir Hussain and Vikku Vinayakram
events.text: English guitarist John McLaughlin formed the band Shakti with Indian musicians, including a young Zakir Hussain on tabla. Their first album was recorded live on 5 July 1975 at Southampton College in New York. They mixed Indian classical music with jazz at breathtaking speed.
events.why: Shakti showed the tabla could lead in a band, not just keep time.

events.title: Tuning a drum, one layer at a time
events.text: Rossing and Sykes followed the tuning of a mridanga, a south Indian drum that shares the tabla's trick. They recorded its sound as more than 100 thin layers of paste were added. Step by step, the overtones moved into harmonic order.
events.why: It showed exactly how the drum maker's patient layering creates the tuning Raman found.

events.title: An electronic tabla
events.text: Raj Narayan was an engineer and a flute player who started Radel in a garage in Bangalore in 1979. In 1987 he showed the Taalmala, an electronic tabla that plays rhythm cycles, by using it to accompany a flute recital. Radel says it was the first such instrument to use software and microprocessors.
events.why: Students everywhere could now practise with a tabla beat at home, even without a drummer.

events.title: Women take the stage
events.who: Dr Aban Mistry (1940–2012) and Anuradha Pal
events.text: For a long time the tabla was played almost only by men. Aban Mistry of Mumbai was among the first women to become a tabla maestro, and she was honoured after her death in 2018. In 1991 the Limca Book of Records listed Anuradha Pal as the first professional female tabla player, and in 1996 she started an all-women band called Stree Shakti.
events.why: They opened a door that many young women drummers have walked through since.

events.title: Planet Drum wins the first world music Grammy
events.who: Mickey Hart, with Zakir Hussain and others
events.text: Grateful Dead drummer Mickey Hart made the album Planet Drum with percussionists from India, Nigeria, Puerto Rico and Brazil. Zakir Hussain played tabla on it. It won the very first Grammy for Best World Music Album.
events.why: It put the tabla at the centre of a new idea: a global conversation between drums.

events.title: Tabla meets drum and bass
events.text: Talvin Singh is a British tabla player and producer from London's Asian Underground scene. His debut album OK mixed tabla with electronic drum and bass, recorded in London, India and Okinawa. It won the 1999 Mercury Prize for the best British album of the year.
events.why: It showed the tabla sounding perfectly at home in electronic dance music.

events.title: Three Grammys in one night
events.text: At the 66th Grammy Awards, Zakir Hussain won three awards: for Shakti's album This Moment, and for the track Pashto and the album As We Speak with Béla Fleck, Edgar Meyer and Rakesh Chaurasia. He became the first musician from India to win three Grammys at one ceremony. India had given him its second-highest civilian honour, the Padma Vibhushan, in 2023.
events.why: It crowned the tabla as a truly global instrument.

events.title: Farewell to Zakir Hussain
events.text: Zakir Hussain, the son and student of Alla Rakha, died in San Francisco at the age of 73. He had played tabla since childhood and worked with musicians from every corner of the world. Tributes poured in from India and far beyond.
events.why: His life carried the Punjab gharana from his father's lessons to stages all over the planet.

people.name: Anokhelal Mishra

people.note: Played with Ravi Shankar at Monterey and Woodstock, and founded a tabla school in Mumbai in 1985.

people.name: Zakir Hussain

facts: The black spot on a tabla, called syahi, is built from many thin layers of a paste containing iron filings.
When Rossing and Sykes watched a mridanga being tuned, more than 100 layers of paste went on the drumhead.
Most drums have messy overtones, but C. V. Raman found that the tabla's loaded head gives five tones in harmonic order, like a string.
The Natya Shastra says the first drums were inspired by heavy rain falling on lotus leaves.
Ram Sahai is said to have played tabla for the Nawab of Lucknow for seven nights in a row when he was about 17.
